title: Tactile Mother-Child Interaction
summary: We are studying the development of C-tactile nerve fibers. These fibers are found almost everywhere in our skin and form a specialized nervous system that allows us to perceive gentle touches such as stroking. Various studies have shown that gentle stroking not only feels good but also has effects on the body. When stroking occurs at the optimal C-tactile speed (1–10 cm/s), the autonomic nervous system calms down: breathing slows, the heart rate decreases, and blood oxygen saturation increases. This effect is particularly interesting in newborns, who often have trouble regulating themselves. In babies who are several weeks or months old, C-tactile-typical calming effects from stroking have already been observed. What we don’t yet know, however, is: When does the C-tactile system begin to develop? Do mothers intuitively use C-tactile-optimized stroking to soothe their babies after birth? To find this out, we are observing 125 mothers with their children after birth. To do this, we are using a combination of observational study and experimental design. First, the child lies on the mother’s upper body, and she has time to hold, stroke, or talk to the child. We observe whether the mothers stroke their babies. Next, the mothers are asked to place their children next to them and stroke them. Afterward, the mothers are asked to place their children next to them and stroke them. Here, we want to know how fast the mothers stroke their children and how the children react to this. We compare this reaction to a baseline condition without physical contact.

interventions.name: Observation of natural mother-infant interaction after birth: Within the first 48 hours after delivery, a 10-minute video recording is made of how mothers naturally touch their infants and how the infants respond. The video data is then coded according to a standardized scheme from the pilot study.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Mother is able to give informed consent; baby's gestational age is at least 37 weeks
Exclusion criteria:
unstable clinical condition
